cards.front: Recall a key point about Supply
cards.back: Supply is the quantity producers are willing and able to sell at a given price over a period of time.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Supply
cards.back: Law of supply: as price rises, quantity supplied rises (positive relationship), shown by an upward-sloping supply curve.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Supply
cards.back: Factors shifting supply: costs of production, technology, taxes and subsidies, number of firms, weather (agriculture).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Supply
cards.back: Movement ALONG the curve = price change. SHIFT of the curve = non-price factor (costs, technology, etc.).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Supply
cards.back: An increase in supply shifts right (more at every price); a decrease shifts left.

cards.front: What should you know about economics exam tips?
cards.back: When analysing supply changes, use the CSE framework: Cost factor (what changed?), Shift direction (right or left?), Effect on market (what happens to equilibrium?).
Change in price of the good itself (e.g. Favourable non-price factor)
Quantity supplied (e.g. Supply at every price)
Higher price = higher profit incentive (e.g. Lower costs = higher profit at each price)
Higher milk price, farms produce more (e.g. New technology increases car output)
Slide along existing curve (e.g. Whole curve moves right)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: A subsidy always benefits consumers because it reduces the price they pay. Correct: While a subsidy lowers consumer prices, the benefits are split between consumers and producers depending on elasticity. If demand is inelastic, producers may keep most of the subsidy as higher profit. Also, consumers bear the cost through taxation.

cards.front: Understanding the Supply Curve and the Law of Supply
cards.back: Supply is the quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to sell at a given price over a period of time. The law of supply states that, ceteris paribus, as the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied increases, and vice versa. This positive relationship is shown by an upward-sloping supply curve.
